zones.label: Column 1
zones.note: Lexical aid consulted after independent scan reading: Entry Words Data of Nippojisho, NINJAL, Hideyuki Ohshima and Taichi Aida, version 202510, supplied page subset, CC BY 4.0. Source: https://www2.ninjal.ac.jp/textdb_dataset/en/nipp/index.html ; license: https://creativecommons.org/licenses/by/4.0/ . The transcription follows the supplied BnF scan; lexical data do not determine damaged glyphs.

lines.note: Sonyeqi is loss and gain, explicitly unpacked as son and tocu. The small separator after i is a comma; the Portuguese gives the same paired contrast.
Sonyô denotes the dignified appearance of a noble or sacred person; Tattoqi catachi gives the Japanese paraphrase. The definition continues on the next row, so peßoa is not an isolated gloss.
The person is noble or holy, with Fotoque as the example. Fotoque is upright Japanese embedded in the otherwise italic Portuguese explanation, not a new headword.
Sonzaxi gives the principal forms of a verb meaning to damage or mistreat. The -aita form is historical morphology and should not be modernized to an expected -shita spelling.
Gotaiuo ſonzaſu applies the verb to the body, meaning to injure or mistreat it. The object particle remains attached to Gotaiuo as printed.
Mal ao corpo completes the preceding Portuguese example: doing harm to the body. This short continuation is a real physical body line.
Sonzǒ is an image or statue of an honored figure; Tattoqi ſugata parallels the appearance gloss above. The final vowel carries a caron in this entry.
Completes the statue definition by naming Fotoque. The Japanese religious term is in upright type within the Portuguese phrase.

Sonzon denotes descendants, and Xixi ſonzõni begins the expression extending through successive generations. The mark in ſonzõni is read as an abbreviation tilde, not the caron of the preceding Sonzǒ entry.
Itarumade completes the Japanese expression, extending to the last descendants. The Portuguese abbreviated deſcẽdentes retains its tilde rather than expanding the omitted nasal.

runs.text: Ley vniuerſal que ha em todas as

lines.note: Soppǒ is explained as a universal law found everywhere. The scan has vniuerſal; the extra u in the provisional vnuiuerſal has no printed counterpart.
Partes completes em todas as partes, meaning in all places. Its separate short line is retained rather than merged with the definition above.
Sǒqe is a cane basket or small hamper, according to both Portuguese nouns. The scan is the authority for the marked first vowel; no modern basket-name spelling is substituted.
Sǒqei is described only as the name of a particular prepared dish. The note does not infer ingredients that the printed definition does not supply.
Soqen is paraphrased as a white silk garment. The Japanese reads Xiroi, not the provisional Xitoi; white in the continuing Portuguese confirms the word identity.

runs.text: ſeda branca que trazem por cima algũs Bonzos

lines.note: The garment is white silk worn over other clothing by some Buddhist monks. The qualification mais mancebos follows on the next physical row.

Mais mancebos completes the description of younger monks. The right-hand (de palha. S. is displaced material completing Sǒqen on the following row, not part of the clothing definition; its physical placement and upright usage label are retained.

Sǒqen, paraphrased as Cuſano noqiba, denotes the eaves of a thatched house. De palha and the written-register label are physically placed at the far right of the preceding row and must not be moved into this line.
Soqi is requesting or wishing, with Coinegǒ as its Japanese equivalent. The caron in Coinegǒ is preserved rather than replacing the historical form with modern spelling.
Soqiſuru is the verbal example for making a request or expressing a wish. Its short standalone physical row belongs to the preceding entry.
Sǒqi and the alternative adjective sǒqina describe something done inattentively or clumsily. The lowercase alternative has a short s in the scan and is not globally changed to long ſ.

Atabalhoadamente completes the careless-action gloss. Sôqina fito introduces a heedless person; the tiny vowel mark is abraded, so the aligned baseline circumflex is retained rather than harmonizing it to sǒqina above. Ho- begins Homem on the next row.
Completes Homem: a flighty, rash or inattentive person. The final adjective is continuous deſatentado, not the provisional split deſa tentado.
Soqiacu is neglect or failure of attention. Ai fedatçu supplies the Japanese paraphrase, and its f is retained as part of fedatçu rather than being confused with long ſ.
Sôqiǒ denotes veneration or respect. Tattomi vyamǒ expresses honoring and revering; the final mark of vyamǒ is read as a caron from the scan.
Fitouo ſôqiǒ ſuru means to honor a person. The Portuguese translation starts Hon- here and finishes on the next physical row.
Rar completes Honrar, followed by venerating someone. The fragment is the continuation of the preceding example, not a separate entry.

Cuſabana identifies flowers of herbaceous plants; the scan supports n rather than the provisional u in the final component. The second Portuguese noun is read fulas, an unusual form retained without lexical modernization; its precise status remains uncertain.
Deruas completes the explanation of flowers growing from herbs. The printed contraction is kept instead of expanding it to de ervas.
Soquai means one's proper or legitimate desire, with Fonmǒ as its Japanese equivalent. The initial is S rather than OCR B, and legi- continues below.
Timo completes legitimo. Soquaiuo toguru is to fulfill one's desire, translated by Comprir and the following row.
Completes the example as fully satisfying one's own desire. The printed desejo spelling is retained independently of the long-s form used elsewhere on the page.
Sôquan and ſôguan are alternative pronunciations of a Buddhist clerical dignity. The scan preserves the q/g contrast and the circumflexes; the alternatives are not separate Portuguese words.
Bonzos completes the definition of a dignity held by Buddhist monks. The brief continuation remains a separate physical line.
Soquat is reviving or rising again, paraphrased by Yomigayeri. The terminal t belongs to the printed Sino-Japanese form; the written-register label S. is upright.
Soquat ſuru gives the corresponding verbal construction for reviving. It continues the preceding entry and does not alter the headword's final consonant.
Sora is air or sky, the literal sense underlying many of the following compounds. Both Portuguese nouns are retained as printed.
Sorabore means pretending to have great love or affection. The Portuguese construction continues directly with amor on the next line.
The gloss completes the idea of feigned affection. The scan reads amor and repeats Soraboreuo, correcting the provisional antor and Sotaboreuo.

runs.text: O ladrar do cão de noite à maneira

lines.note: Soraboye is a dog's night barking in the manner of a howl. The headword starts at the normal entry margin, and O ladrar has a real word space.

runs.text: de vyuo. No Cami ſe diz,

lines.note: De vyuo completes the comparison to howling. The Portuguese then identifies Nagaboye as the term used in Cami, before introducing a second regional name below.
The Ximo regional equivalent is Tatçuboye. The initial of Ximo is visibly capitalized; the Japanese name remains upright within this continuation of the Portuguese comparison.

runs.text: O eſtar em pee nalgum lugar ſoſpei-

lines.note: Soradachi means standing idly in a suspicious place. Enlargement establishes two e-types in the historical spelling pee, restoring the second one omitted by the provisional text; ſoſpei- continues on the next row.
The gloss completes standing without doing anything. Soradachiuo ſu- begins the illustrative verb phrase and keeps its printed terminal hyphen.
Ru completes ſu-ru. The Portuguese introduces the Ximo equivalent Sozorodachi, whose last syllable is physically continued on the next row.
Chi ſuru completes Sozoroda-chi ſuru from the preceding row. It belongs to the regional equivalent, not to a separate headword.
The worn headword reads Soradamari, meaning dissimulation, not the provisional Buracanran. Its example breaks as Soradama- at the column foot and resumes with ri xite iru at the top of column 2.
Ri xite iru completes Soradama-ri xite iru across the column boundary. The Portuguese describes remaining dissimulating and malicious; this continuation is indented like other example continuations.
Soradamari, u, atta supplies the principal forms of the verb meaning to feign or dissimulate. It is separate from the noun entry that ended column 1.
Soradanomi denotes vain hopes. The Portuguese Vaãs preserves the tilde over the second a rather than being modernized to vãs.
Soradarumi is explicitly equated with Soradamari and glossed as pretense or dissimulation. The synonym is Japanese apparatus, not an embedded Portuguese term for typeface indexing.
The continuation finishes dißimulação and introduces Soradarumi ſuru, to dissimulate. Its translation divides Fin-gir over two physical rows.
Gir completes Fingir, followed by the synonymous Portuguese dißimular. The indented continuation must not be treated as a new entry.
Soragocoro is a false or dissembling heart. Refalſado is retained as the printed historical adjective rather than modernized.
Soragoto means a lie. The compact one-word Portuguese definition is complete on this row.

Sôrai is coming at a run. The scan visibly prints Vaxiri, although the meaning suggests the familiar running verb; that apparent printed anomaly is retained rather than silently changed to Faxiri. S. is an upright written-register label.
Sǒrai is an inflected copular or existential form equated with Soro. All three marked vowels in its principal forms have carons in the scan.
Completes the list of copular and existential senses and labels the usage as written. The final S. is upright rather than part of the italic gloss.
Sorajeimon denotes a false or feigned oath. The Japanese form and the Portuguese juramento refer to the same act of swearing.
Sorajini is feigned death. The Portuguese has a space in Morte fingida; the Japanese example breaks at the printed ſu-.
Ru completes ſuru, and the translation explains pretending to be dead. The grave accent in eſtà is preserved from the supplied form and scan.
Sorairo is light blue, literally the sky color in the Japanese compound. Azul claro provides a complete gloss.

runs.text: Vendo, fazer ou fingir que não vẽ.

lines.note: Sorame is pretending not to see something one actually sees. The scan does not show the provisional extra comma after fazer; the nasal abbreviation in vẽ is retained.
Sorameuo ſuru gives the action of pretending not to see. Vt is italic apparatus; the Japanese example is upright.
Sorami means looking lightly or without attention. The Portuguese distinguishes this inattentive seeing from deliberate pretense in the preceding entry.
Soramixite iru is remaining in that inattentive state of looking. Apli- continues as cação on the next row, preserving the physical word division.
Cação completes aplicação, attention or application. The one-word fragment belongs to the example's translation.

runs.text: Lugar de muitas eruas cheiroſas i, õde

lines.note: Sôran is a place rich in fragrant herbs. The explanatory i, begins a restatement, and õde retains the nasal abbreviation visible in the print.

runs.text: ha quantidade de huãs certas eruas cheiroſas

lines.note: The restatement specifies a quantity of certain fragrant herbs. The tilde in huãs is over the a and is not moved to the preceding vowel.
Da China identifies the herbs as Chinese. It completes the description without supplying a species name absent from the source.
Soranaqi is feigned weeping, and Soranaqi ſuru gives the associated action. The noun and example agree in their naqi component.
Soranji denotes learning by heart or reciting from memory. De còr carries the printed grave accent; the principal forms remain in their historical spelling.

runs.text: algũa couſa de còr, ou de memoria.

lines.note: The gloss continues with saying something by heart or from memory. The nasal abbreviation in algũa is preserved, not expanded.

runs.text: Pera cima, ou pera o ceo. Vt,

lines.note: Soraſama means upward or toward the sky. The example introduced by Vt follows on the next row.

Camiua ſoraſamaye voi nobotta describes the hair rising upward, as confirmed by the Portuguese translation below. Camiua here is part of the Japanese example, not the regional name Cami; Feiq. is a separate upright citation label.

runs.text: Lib. 1. Os cabelos eſtauão hirtos pera cima.

lines.note: The citation specifies book 1 and translates the hair as standing erect upward. Lib. 1. belongs to the italic bibliographical apparatus following upright Feiq.

runs.text: O dißimular como quem não ſabe,

lines.note: Soratoboqe means feigning ignorance or incomprehension. The definition continues below rather than ending at ſabe.

runs.text: ou não entende o que lhe dizẽ, &c. Vt,

lines.note: Completes pretending not to understand what is said. So- begins the Japanese example and is entirely upright; the provisional italic o split is unsupported by the type.
Ratoboqeuo ſuru completes So-ratoboqeuo ſuru across the physical break. The whole expression exemplifies feigned incomprehension.

runs.text: O aſouiar ao ar como quem eſta triſte,

lines.note: Soravſo denotes whistling into the air in a sad or pensive manner. The initial v supplies the vowel of the Japanese compound and is not a Portuguese consonant to normalize.
The pensive qualification is completed, followed by Soravſouo fuqu, to whistle in this fashion. Aſo- begins the Portuguese verb across the line break.
Viar completes Aſouiar and specifies whistling in the manner just described. The short translation remains a separate body row.

runs.text: Cantiga que hum canta aßi como por

lines.note: Soravta is a song sung jokingly or in pretense. The following lines explain that no such established song or tune exists.

runs.text: zombaria, ou fingidamente, não auendo tal

lines.note: The gloss continues with singing in jest or pretense, despite there being no such song. The final word is tal, including the l omitted by the provisional text.
Cantiga, nem toada completes the statement that neither that song nor its melody exists. It belongs to the preceding account of improvised or pretended singing.
Soravtagai is unwarranted doubt or suspicion of someone. The scan supports duuidar and deſconfiar, correcting the missing letters in duidar and deſconfar.
The doubt is without reason or foundation. This qualification distinguishes the entry from ordinary justified suspicion.
Soraxi gives the transitive verb for bending or arching parts of the body or another object. The principal forms are retained without modernizing the historical -aita ending.
Completes the general object of bending and introduces Teuo ſora-ſu. The example concerns bending the hands and is physically divided here.

runs.text: Arcar as mãos, ou botar as palmas das

lines.note: The example describes arching the hands or turning the palms outward. The row ends after das and must continue into mãos on the next row.
Mãos completes the outward-palms translation. Qiuo ſoraſu introduces bending wood, and Entor- begins its Portuguese rendering.
Tar completes Entortar, bending or warping a stick. Tacauo ſo- begins a different example involving a falcon, continued below.
Raſu completes the falcon example, glossed as letting the falcon escape. The distinct contextual sense is preserved rather than forced into the preceding wood-bending sense.

runs.text: Ponta da bainha que ſobeja fora da

lines.note: Sorazaya is the surplus tip of a scabbard extending beyond the sword. The definition continues with catana on the next page; the bottom Catana. is a catchword, not an additional body line.
